title: HIVE Doctor — Overdose Prevention & Harm Reduction Reference
policy: This section exists to SAVE LIVES: to recognize and respond to overdose, to flag deadly combinations and the tolerance trap, and to connect people to help and to specialized harm-reduction services. It deliberately does NOT give recreational doses for illicit or street drugs — street supply is contaminated and unpredictable (fentanyl is widespread), so no amount is 'safe', and a number gives false confidence. For substance-specific safer-use guidance, use the specialized services listed here. Nothing here is a substitute for emergency care or a clinician.
universal_rules: If someone is unresponsive, breathing slowly/irregularly, or not breathing — call 911 (or local emergency) now. Give naloxone if opioids are possible; start rescue breaths/CPR as directed.
NEVER use alone. If you use, have someone with you or use a 'never use alone' phone line so someone can call help.
The TOLERANCE TRAP kills: after any break (days clean, detox, jail, illness, a new batch), your old 'usual amount' can be a fatal dose. Restart far lower than before.
NEVER mix depressants: opioids + benzodiazepines + alcohol + other sedatives stack up and stop breathing. Most overdose deaths involve a mix.
Assume illicit drugs may contain fentanyl or other potent adulterants. Use fentanyl test strips, and carry naloxone — it reverses opioid overdose.
Good Samaritan laws in many places protect you from certain charges when you call 911 for an overdose. Calling is the right move.

overdose_guides.class: Opioids (heroin, fentanyl, oxycodone, morphine, methadone, etc.)
overdose_signs: Slow, shallow, or stopped breathing (the thing that kills)
Unresponsive, limp, gurgling or snoring sounds
response: Give naloxone (nasal or injectable) per the kit; repeat every 2–3 minutes if no response.
Give rescue breaths; start CPR if not breathing and you're trained/directed.
Put them in the recovery position; stay — overdose can return as naloxone wears off.
key_dangers: Mixing with benzodiazepines or alcohol greatly raises the risk (and naloxone does not reverse those).
Tolerance loss after any break is a leading cause of fatal overdose.
overdose_guides.note: Carry naloxone if you or someone near you uses opioids — it's free in many places and reverses opioid overdose.

response: Recovery position to protect the airway from vomit.
Do not leave them to 'sleep it off' if breathing is abnormal or they can't be roused.
Naloxone won't reverse these, but give it anyway if opioids might also be involved.
key_dangers: Combining with opioids or other depressants stops breathing.
Stopping heavy alcohol or benzodiazepine use SUDDENLY can cause dangerous withdrawal and seizures — medical help is needed to stop safely.
GHB has a very narrow margin and a steep overdose curve.
overdose_guides.note: Alcohol/benzo withdrawal can be life-threatening — never quit heavy use cold turkey without medical support.

overdose_signs: Very high body temperature (overheating), heavy sweating
response: Call 911 — stimulant overdose can cause heart attack, stroke, or fatal overheating.
Move to a cool place, remove excess clothing, cool them down, offer sips of water if alert (MDMA overheating).
Keep them calm; protect from injury during a seizure.
Do not assume it will pass — chest pain or seizure is an emergency.
key_dangers: Overheating and dehydration (especially MDMA at events) — but also DON'T over-drink water, which can be fatal with MDMA.
Hidden heart conditions; mixing stimulants strains the heart.
Contamination with fentanyl or other substances.
overdose_guides.note: There's no reversal drug for stimulants — cooling, calming, and emergency care are the response.

overdose_signs: Unresponsive or unable to move/protect airway ('k-hole')
Dangerously high blood pressure or heart rate (PCP)
response: Call 911 if unresponsive, vomiting while out, having a seizure, or with chest pain.
Keep the environment calm and safe; reduce stimulation.
key_dangers: Loss of coordination/consciousness leads to choking or injury.
Severe psychological distress needs calm support and, if unsafe, medical help.
overdose_guides.note: For a difficult psychological experience, a calm, safe setting and reassurance help; seek medical help if there's danger to self or others.

safer_use.title: Safer use & infection prevention (needle exchange / supervised consumption basics)
safer_use.intent: The core public-health harm-reduction practices that needle-exchange and supervised consumption services provide — they dramatically cut overdose deaths, HIV, hepatitis C, and serious infections. This is infection-prevention and connection to services, not a guide on how much to use.
principles: Use a NEW, STERILE needle/syringe every single time. Never reuse your own and never share — sharing spreads HIV and hepatitis C.
Never share ANY equipment: needles, cookers, filters, water, ties, pipes, or straws. Hepatitis C survives on equipment and spreads easily.
Get free sterile supplies and sharps containers from a needle-exchange / harm-reduction program; many also give out naloxone and fentanyl test strips.
Use a supervised consumption site where available — trained staff, clean supplies, and someone present to reverse an overdose. These sites have never had an on-site death.
Wash hands and clean the skin with an alcohol swab before injecting, to prevent abscesses and bloodstream infections.
Use your own clean water; do not lick needles or equipment.
Rotate sites and avoid damaged skin; never inject into a red, swollen, or painful area.
Dispose of used needles in a sharps container or a rigid sealed container — return them to the exchange; never leave them loose.
Do not use alone; carry naloxone; use fentanyl test strips; and remember the tolerance trap after any break.
infection_warning_signs: Abscess: a red, hot, swollen, painful lump at an injection site — see a clinician; it may need draining or antibiotics.
Spreading redness, red streaks, fever, or feeling very unwell — possible serious bloodstream infection; seek care urgently.
Endocarditis (heart-valve infection): fever, chills, night sweats, breathlessness, and fatigue after injecting — a medical EMERGENCY.
A wound that will not heal, or numbness or coldness in a limb after a missed injection — get medical help.
safer_use.testing_note: Where drug-checking services exist (at many harm-reduction sites and some events), use them — they can detect fentanyl and other adulterants before use. Fentanyl test strips are a simple at-home option.
safer_use.getting_help: Needle exchanges and supervised consumption sites also connect people to HIV/HCV testing, wound care, naloxone, and — whenever wanted — treatment and support. Asking about treatment is always available and never required to get clean supplies.
